CHAPTER 2.1 · LEARNING AREA 2

CHAPTER 2.1 · LEARNING AREA 2 · NOVEMBER

Fractions

Half a pizza, a quarter of the class, three eighths of a litre of milk: when you divide a whole into equal parts, you get fractions. You learn to draw fractions and read them off, to calculate parts of quantities, to simplify and expand fractions and to find out which of two fractions is bigger.

12 LESSONS3 UNITS
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • show fractions on circles, rectangles and solids and read them off
  • calculate parts of amounts and quantities, for example $\tfrac{2}{3}$ of 27
  • simplify and expand fractions, distinguish proper and improper fractions
  • show fractions on the number ray, compare them and put them in order
CHECK-IN: CAN YOU ALREADY DO THIS?

What is half of 100?

$100 \div 2$

How many minutes are a quarter of an hour?

$60 \div 4$

What is the highest common factor of 12 and 18?

$T_{12}$ and $T_{18}$ have 1, 2, 3 and 6 in common.

FOLDING PAPER

Fold a sheet of paper in half once, twice, three times and open it again.

  • How many equal parts do you get each time? What is one part called?
  • Colour in three parts of the sheet folded three times. What fraction have you coloured?
→ Unit 1

  • Who has eaten the most? Draw the bars.
→ Unit 2

Class 5a: 3 out of 4 came by bike. Class 5b: 5 out of 7.

  • In which class is the proportion of cyclists bigger? How can you decide?

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1Fractions as parts

Folding once gives 2 halves, folding twice 4 quarters, folding three times 8 eighths. Three coloured eighths are the fraction $\tfrac{3}{8}$, read “three eighths”.

The denominator below the fraction bar names how many equal parts the whole is divided into. The numerator above it numbers how many of these parts are meant. What matters is: the parts must be equal in size.

KEY POINT · FRACTION AND PART

In the fraction $\dfrac{3}{8}$, 3 is the numerator: you take this many parts. 8 is the denominator: the whole is divided into this many equal parts.

A fraction of an amount or quantity: first divide by the denominator, then multiply by the numerator.

$\tfrac{2}{3}$ of 27 marbles: $27 \div 3 = 9$, $9 \cdot 2 = 18$ marbles.

Fractions with names: $\tfrac12$ a half, $\tfrac13$ a third, $\tfrac14$ a quarter, $\tfrac15$ a fifth, $\tfrac{1}{10}$ a tenth, $\tfrac{1}{100}$ a hundredth.

Unit fractions have the numerator 1. Every fraction is a multiple of a unit fraction: $\tfrac38 = 3 \cdot \tfrac18$.

INTERACTIVE · FRACTIONS AS PICTURES
EXAMPLE 1 · A FRACTION OF A QUANTITY

What is $\tfrac34$ of 2 hours?

2 hours = 120 minutes. $120 \div 4 = 30$, $30 \cdot 3 = 90$.

90 minutes, i.e. an hour and a half

EXAMPLE 2 · FROM THE PART TO THE WHOLE

$\tfrac25$ of a route is 12 km. How long is the whole route?

2 fifths are 12 km, so one fifth is 6 km. Five fifths are $5 \cdot 6$ km.

30 km

EXERCISES

Draw a rectangle of 3 by 4 squares and colour a) $\tfrac{1}{4}$   b) $\tfrac{2}{3}$   c) $\tfrac{5}{12}$ of it. How many squares is that each time?

a) 3 squares   b) 8 squares   c) 5 squares

Calculate: a) $\tfrac{1}{5}$ of €40   b) $\tfrac{3}{4}$ of 1 kg   c) $\tfrac{2}{3}$ of 27   d) $\tfrac{5}{6}$ of an hour

a) €8   b) 750 g   c) 18   d) 50 minutes

There are 28 pupils in a class; $\tfrac{3}{7}$ of them are boys. How many boys and how many girls are there?

$28 \div 7 = 4$, $4 \cdot 3 = 12$ boys and 16 girls.

Paul has already read $\tfrac{3}{8}$ of his book; that is 96 pages. How many pages does the book have? How many are still to go?

One eighth is $96 \div 3 = 32$ pages. The book has $8 \cdot 32 = 256$ pages; 160 are still to go.

A cube is built from 27 small cubes. What fraction of the small cubes lies a) in the top layer   b) exactly in the middle, invisible from outside?

a) 9 of 27, so $\tfrac{9}{27} = \tfrac13$   b) 1 of 27, so $\tfrac{1}{27}$

Lena spends half of her pocket money on a book and a third of the rest on ice cream. After that she still has €6. How much pocket money did she have?

Work backwards: the €6 are two thirds of the rest.

The rest before the ice cream: €9. That is half, so she had €18. Check: $18 - 9 - 3 = 6$.

TEST YOURSELF!

What is $\tfrac23$ of 27?

$27 \div 3 \cdot 2$

How many minutes are $\tfrac34$ of an hour?

$60 \div 4 \cdot 3$

$\tfrac25$ of a route is 12 km. How long is it?

one fifth is 6 km

UNIT 24 LESSONS

2Simplifying and expanding

Mia, Ben and Lena have eaten the same amount of chocolate: $\tfrac24 = \tfrac36 = \tfrac48$, half the bar each time. The fractions look different, but they describe the same part.

If you cut every part into 2 equal pieces, the number of parts and the number of parts taken both double; the fraction stays the same. This is called expanding. If, the other way round, you put parts together, it is called simplifying.

KEY POINT · SIMPLIFYING AND EXPANDING

Expanding: multiply the numerator and the denominator by the same number: $\tfrac{3}{4} = \tfrac{3 \cdot 5}{4 \cdot 5} = \tfrac{15}{20}$

Simplifying: divide the numerator and the denominator by the same number: $\tfrac{18}{24} = \tfrac{18 \div 6}{24 \div 6} = \tfrac{3}{4}$

The value of the fraction does not change. If you divide by the highest common factor, the fraction is fully simplified.

Proper fractions are less than 1 ($\tfrac34$), improper fractions are at least 1 ($\tfrac54$, $\tfrac44$). Improper fractions can be written as a mixed number: $\tfrac{7}{4} = 1\tfrac{3}{4}$.

Trap: you must not add or subtract numbers. $\tfrac{3}{4}$ is not equal to $\tfrac{3 + 1}{4 + 1} = \tfrac{4}{5}$.

Whole numbers as fractions: $3 = \tfrac{3}{1} = \tfrac{6}{2} = \tfrac{12}{4}$.

INTERACTIVE · EXPANDING AND SIMPLIFYING IN PICTURES

Tap “Expand by 2”: in the rectangle every part is halved horizontally. The coloured area stays the same size.

EXAMPLE 3 · SIMPLIFYING FULLY

Simplify $\tfrac{36}{48}$ fully.

Step by step: $\tfrac{36}{48} = \tfrac{18}{24} = \tfrac{9}{12} = \tfrac{3}{4}$, or straight away by the highest common factor 12.

$\tfrac{3}{4}$

EXAMPLE 4 · TO A GIVEN DENOMINATOR

Expand $\tfrac{2}{5}$ to the denominator 35.

$35 \div 5 = 7$, so expand by 7: $\tfrac{2 \cdot 7}{5 \cdot 7}$.

$\tfrac{14}{35}$

EXERCISES

a) $\tfrac36, \tfrac{5}{10}, \tfrac{10}{20}$   b) $\tfrac{9}{12}, \tfrac{15}{20}, \tfrac{30}{40}$   c) $\tfrac{6}{21}, \tfrac{10}{35}, \tfrac{20}{70}$

a) $\tfrac34$   b) $\tfrac35$   c) $\tfrac23$   d) $\tfrac34$   e) $\tfrac{7}{10}$

a) $2\tfrac14$   b) $3\tfrac25$   c) $\tfrac73$   d) $\tfrac{11}{2}$

Which fractions are equal? $\tfrac{4}{6}$, $\tfrac{10}{15}$, $\tfrac{6}{8}$, $\tfrac{12}{18}$, $\tfrac{9}{12}$, $\tfrac{14}{21}$

$\tfrac46 = \tfrac{10}{15} = \tfrac{12}{18} = \tfrac{14}{21} = \tfrac23$ and $\tfrac68 = \tfrac{9}{12} = \tfrac34$

Fill the gaps: a) $\tfrac{3}{5} = \tfrac{▢}{40}$   b) $\tfrac{▢}{9} = \tfrac{20}{36}$   c) $\tfrac{12}{▢} = \tfrac{3}{8}$

a) 24   b) 5   c) 32

Find a fraction with the denominator 24 that lies between $\tfrac{1}{3}$ and $\tfrac{1}{2}$. How many are there?

$\tfrac13 = \tfrac{8}{24}$ and $\tfrac12 = \tfrac{12}{24}$. In between lie $\tfrac{9}{24}$, $\tfrac{10}{24}$ and $\tfrac{11}{24}$: three fractions.

$\tfrac34 = \tfrac{▢}{20}$. Which numerator is missing?

expanded by 5

By which number do you simplify $\tfrac{36}{48}$ fully in one step?

the highest common factor of 36 and 48

$\tfrac98 = 1\tfrac18$ is greater than 1.

UNIT 34 LESSONS

3Comparing fractions on the number ray

In 5a $\tfrac34$ come by bike, in 5b $\tfrac57$. Expanded to the denominator 28: $\tfrac{21}{28}$ and $\tfrac{20}{28}$. Now you see it at once: the proportion in 5a is a little bigger.

On the number ray you divide the distance from 0 to 1 into as many equal parts as the denominator says. Fractions with the denominator 4 lie on the quarters, $\tfrac44 = 1$ lies exactly on the 1, and improper fractions lie to the right of it.

KEY POINT · COMPARING FRACTIONS
  • Same denominators: the fraction with the bigger numerator is bigger. $\tfrac{5}{9} > \tfrac{4}{9}$
  • Same numerators: the fraction with the smaller denominator is bigger, because its parts are bigger. $\tfrac{3}{5} > \tfrac{3}{8}$
  • Otherwise: expand both to a common denominator, then compare the numerators.

A quick trick: compare with $\tfrac12$ or with 1. $\tfrac{3}{7}$ is less than a half, $\tfrac{5}{9}$ more. So $\tfrac37 < \tfrac59$.

Common denominator: the product of the denominators always works. Often a smaller number that is a multiple of both denominators is enough: for 4 and 6, 12 will do.

INTERACTIVE · TWO FRACTIONS ON THE NUMBER RAY
EXAMPLE 5 · ORDERING

Put in order of size: $\tfrac{2}{3}$, $\tfrac{5}{6}$, $\tfrac{7}{12}$, $\tfrac{3}{4}$

Common denominator 12: $\tfrac{8}{12}$, $\tfrac{10}{12}$, $\tfrac{7}{12}$, $\tfrac{9}{12}$.

$\tfrac{7}{12} < \tfrac{2}{3} < \tfrac{3}{4} < \tfrac{5}{6}$

EXAMPLE 6 · THE MIDDLE

Which fraction lies exactly halfway between $\tfrac{1}{4}$ and $\tfrac{1}{2}$?

Expanded to eighths: $\tfrac{2}{8}$ and $\tfrac{4}{8}$. Exactly in between lies $\tfrac{3}{8}$.

$\tfrac{3}{8}$

EXERCISES

Draw a number ray from 0 to 2, 12 cm long. Mark: $\tfrac{1}{2}$, $\tfrac{2}{3}$, $\tfrac{5}{6}$, $\tfrac{4}{3}$, $1\tfrac{1}{2}$.

1 cm corresponds to $\tfrac16$. So $\tfrac12$ at 3 cm, $\tfrac23$ at 4 cm, $\tfrac56$ at 5 cm, $\tfrac43$ at 8 cm, $1\tfrac12$ at 9 cm.

Fill in $<$, $>$ or $=$: a) $\tfrac{3}{7}$ ▢ $\tfrac{5}{7}$   b) $\tfrac{2}{5}$ ▢ $\tfrac{2}{9}$   c) $\tfrac{4}{6}$ ▢ $\tfrac{6}{9}$   d) $\tfrac{5}{4}$ ▢ $\tfrac{9}{10}$

a) $<$   b) $>$   c) $=$   d) $>$ (greater than 1 against less than 1)

Compare with a common denominator: a) $\tfrac{3}{4}$ and $\tfrac{4}{5}$   b) $\tfrac{5}{6}$ and $\tfrac{7}{9}$   c) $\tfrac{7}{10}$ and $\tfrac{2}{3}$

a) $\tfrac{15}{20} < \tfrac{16}{20}$   b) $\tfrac{15}{18} > \tfrac{14}{18}$   c) $\tfrac{21}{30} > \tfrac{20}{30}$

In a survey, 12 out of 20 pupils in 5a like maths best, and in 5b 15 out of 24. Where is the proportion bigger?

$\tfrac{12}{20} = \tfrac35 = \tfrac{24}{40}$ and $\tfrac{15}{24} = \tfrac58 = \tfrac{25}{40}$: in 5b, just.

Which is bigger: $\tfrac{99}{100}$ or $\tfrac{100}{101}$? Give a reason without expanding.

How much is missing to make 1 in each case?

To make 1, $\tfrac{1}{100}$ and $\tfrac{1}{101}$ are missing. Because $\tfrac{1}{101}$ is smaller, $\tfrac{100}{101}$ lies closer to 1 and is bigger.

TEST YOURSELF!

Which fraction is bigger?

the same numerators; fifths are bigger

What is the lowest common denominator of $\tfrac{3}{4}$ and $\tfrac{5}{6}$?

12 is the lowest common multiple of 4 and 6.

Which fraction lies exactly halfway between $\tfrac14$ and $\tfrac12$?

$\tfrac28$ and $\tfrac48$, in between $\tfrac38$

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

What fraction of the day has passed? a) at 6 am   b) at 6 pm   c) at 4 pm. Simplify fully.

a) $\tfrac{6}{24} = \tfrac14$   b) $\tfrac{18}{24} = \tfrac34$   c) $\tfrac{16}{24} = \tfrac23$

Connecting with chapter 1.3: Why can a fraction with a prime number as its denominator, for example $\tfrac{4}{7}$, not be simplified as long as the numerator is smaller than the denominator?

The only factors of 7 are 1 and 7. A numerator between 1 and 6 is not divisible by 7, so there is no common factor except 1.

A glass is $\tfrac{2}{3}$ full of juice; that is 200 ml. How much does the full glass hold? How much space is left?

One third is 100 ml: it holds 300 ml, and 100 ml is free.

Three loaves are to be shared fairly between five people. The ancient Egyptians would have given each one half a loaf and a tenth of a loaf. Is that right? How much does each person get?

Each person gets $\tfrac35$ of a loaf. $\tfrac12 + \tfrac{1}{10} = \tfrac{5}{10} + \tfrac{1}{10} = \tfrac{6}{10} = \tfrac35$. It is right: five half loaves and five tenths need exactly $2\tfrac12 + \tfrac12 = 3$ loaves.

EXCURSIONHISTORY

Fractions on the Nile

About 3,500 years ago an Egyptian scribe called Ahmes wrote a collection of mathematical problems on a papyrus roll. In doing so he copied an even older book. The roll is about five metres long in all and is known today as the Rhind Papyrus, after the Scot Alexander Henry Rhind, who bought it in Luxor in 1858. Today it is in the British Museum in London.

The Egyptians calculated almost only with unit fractions, that is fractions with the numerator 1. The only exception was $\tfrac23$. They wrote all other parts as a sum of different unit fractions: $\tfrac{2}{5} = \tfrac{1}{3} + \tfrac{1}{15}$ or $\tfrac{3}{5} = \tfrac12 + \tfrac{1}{10}$. At the beginning of the papyrus there is a whole table of these. Many problems are about sharing out bread and beer among workers.

Try it yourself: how can you write $\tfrac{3}{4}$ as a sum of two different unit fractions?

Source: British Museum, Rhind Mathematical Papyrus (EA 10057 and EA 10058), around 1550 BC. G. Robins, C. Shute: The Rhind Mathematical Papyrus. British Museum Publications, London 1987.

Solution: $\tfrac34 = \tfrac12 + \tfrac14$

LOOKING BACKTHE ESSENTIALS AT A GLANCE

FRACTION

Denominator: divide into this many equal parts · numerator: take this many parts

$\tfrac38$: three of eight equal parts

CALCULATING A PART

divide by the denominator, multiply by the numerator

$\tfrac23$ of 27: $27 \div 3 \cdot 2 = 18$

SIMPLIFYING AND EXPANDING

Divide or multiply the numerator and denominator by the same number; the value stays the same.

$\tfrac{18}{24} = \tfrac34 = \tfrac{15}{20}$

PROPER, IMPROPER, MIXED

proper: less than 1 · improper: at least 1

$\tfrac74 = 1\tfrac34$

COMPARING

bring to a common denominator, then compare the numerators

$\tfrac34 = \tfrac{21}{28} > \tfrac{20}{28} = \tfrac57$
